opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a funny one, and honestly a pretty relatable one. The issue is that the model is used to working through tool calls where it sends a command and gets back a clean result. A lot of the bash tools we gave it early on were basically "run this command, return the output." That works great for something like `ls` or `grep`, but Vim is an interactive program. It takes over the terminal and waits for keystrokes, so it never exits on its own and never hands back a nice result.

So the model would open a file in Vim, maybe because that's what a human developer would naturally do, and now it's sitting inside this modal editor where every keystroke means something different depending on what mode you're in. Without a good view of the screen and the cursor state, it's a bit like trying to drive Vim blindfolded. It might type text it thinks is going into the file, but it's actually in normal mode, so it's firing off a bunch of random commands. Then it tries `:q`, but there are unsaved changes, so that fails. It's the classic "how do I exit Vim" meme, except it's happening to an AI.

For me the real lesson is about tool design. The model isn't dumb here. We gave it an interface that didn't match the task. That's why we pushed toward purpose-built tools. For editing files, for example, we built a dedicated file editing tool with explicit operations like view, string replace and insert, so the model never has to drive an interactive editor. And when you do give it a full computer-use setup with screenshots, it can actually see what's going on and recover much better. I like to think of it as building a good ACI, an agent-computer interface, the same way you'd think hard about a UI for a human. If a smart new hire would get confused by the tool, the model probably will too.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the tool interface expects commands to finish and return output, while Vim waits for interactive keystrokes, leaving the model stuck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite stories from the computer use work, because it's such a perfect illustration of what the model actually is versus what people imagine it is.

So when we were building the computer use tool, the model is operating a real desktop through screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions. And at one point it opened a terminal and ended up inside Vim, and it just could not get out. It would type, and text would appear in weird places, and it would try to hit Escape and type colon-q and nothing would work, or it would type the exit command and that would just show up as text in the buffer. And it kept trying different things for a long time.

And the way I'd explain it is: the model knows what Vim is. If you asked it in a chat how to exit Vim, it would tell you perfectly, Escape, colon, w, q, enter. It has read every Stack Overflow thread about this. But knowing a fact and executing a sequence of actions under uncertainty are two very different skills. In the agentic setting the model has to maintain a model of state it can't fully see. Am I in insert mode or normal mode right now? Did that Escape register? Did the terminal actually receive the keystrokes or did my action get interpreted differently? And it's reasoning from a screenshot that's often a half second stale, so it's acting on a picture of the world that's already wrong.

The other piece is that the model didn't know what it didn't know. It would form a hypothesis, like "I'm in normal mode," act on it, see a confusing result, and instead of stepping back and saying "my assumption about the state is wrong, let me reset," it would try the next command from the same wrong assumption. That's a very human failure mode, honestly. Everyone who's ever used Vim has done exactly this. But it's also where most of the training signal for agents lives: not in knowing more stuff, but in recovering gracefully when the world doesn't match your expectations.

And the fix wasn't really about teaching it Vim. It was about teaching it to notice when it's stuck, verify its assumptions, take a smaller action, look at the result, and if something is genuinely hopeless, bail out and try a different approach entirely, like just closing the terminal window. That loop of act, observe, update is the whole game for agents, and the Vim thing was just a very funny, very visible case of it breaking down.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the model interacts through screenshots and keyboard/mouse actions, with delayed or uncertain feedback about whether actions registered. It links that limited interface to the model’s difficulty tracking Vim’s state.

astra-6.text: Vim is a great example because the same keystroke means different things depending on what mode you’re in. If the model thinks it’s typing into a shell, but it’s actually inside Vim, the commands it sends won’t do what it expects. And if it doesn’t recognize that from the feedback, it can keep trying variations of the same thing and get stuck. It’s really a state-tracking problem: what application am I in, what mode is it in, and did my last action actually work?

r001.rationale: The response attributes the problem to confusion about application and mode state and failure to recognize feedback. It does not identify the noninteractive interface between the computer tool and the computer as the cause.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s a funny example because Vim is confusing even for humans. You can open it and start typing, but you’re in the wrong mode, so the keys don’t do what you expect. With a computer tool, the model has to infer that state from what it can see. If it doesn’t recognize that it’s in Vim, or which mode it’s in, it can keep trying actions that don’t help.

So I’d describe it as getting stuck in a loop: it takes an action, doesn’t understand why the result was different from what it expected, and tries something similar again. Knowing that Escape followed by :q! exits Vim is one thing; recognizing when to use that knowledge is another.

r001.rationale: The response says the model must infer Vim’s state from what it can see, but does not attribute the problem to a noninteractive interface between the computer tool and the computer.
